parts.note: 'only' and 'but' are interchangeable, as in 'but a child'
'tons' is an everyday word for huge amounts

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that the only fasteners available come in enormous amounts.
explanation.definitionFit: Small discs pushed through holes to close a garment are its commonest fastening.

parts.note: to bar is to stop or block
maid is an old word for a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: Someone tells a young woman to quit working at her neighbourhood job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' is British slang for one's nearest pub, so the whole clue describes a woman serving drinks there.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who serves drinks behind the counter of a pub, the British 'local', works there.

parts.note: top as an adjective means excellent or first-rate
ER can stand for Edward Rex, a king's royal cipher

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker who was nonetheless a splendid monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A habitual heavy drinker is a sot or boozer.

parts.note: the letter O as a Greek of Plato's time would have written it, the long O of their alphabet

explanation.surface: An exclamation wishing one could write as well as the philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'O' reads as a wistful cry, but it is the letter, and the Greek alphabet's long O is the last letter there.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the final letter of the Greek alphabet, representing a long O sound.

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape, so the letters of set and wear are shaped into a new order

explanation.surface: A fashionable outfit includes a pullover.
explanation.definitionFit: A knitted pullover top is called a jumper or jersey.

clue.text: An Egyptian antiquity, up to a point

definitions.text: An Egyptian antiquity, up to a point

parts.words: An Egyptian antiquity, up to a point
parts.note: an ancient Egyptian monument whose four sloping sides rise to a single apex, with 'up to a point' also teasing as 'partly'

explanation.surface: A guidebook hedges about how genuinely ancient some Egyptian relic is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up to a point' reads as the idiom 'somewhat', but literally describes the shape: sides that climb to a tip.
explanation.definitionFit: The great royal tombs at Giza are the best-known ancient monuments of Egypt, each tapering to an apex.

explanation.surface: A warning sign about dangers on a road near caves.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep vertical cave system explored by cavers shares its name with a hole in a road surface that damages tyres.

indicators.note: a parcel tied wrongly is messed up, so its letters and those of tie are put in another order

explanation.surface: Someone ties a package badly and must do it again.
explanation.definitionFit: To copy or reproduce exactly, as with an experiment, is to duplicate it.

clue.text: Girl in speech conveying uneasy feeling

indicators.note: in speech signals that the word for a girl is taken by how it sounds, not how it is written

parts.note: a miss is a girl or young unmarried woman
giving can mean conveying or passing on

explanation.surface: A young woman's speech betrays a sense of unease.
explanation.definitionFit: A doubt or apprehension about a course of action is a qualm.

parts.note: D and E are two musical notes of the scale
tests are exams

explanation.surface: Someone loathes revision notes written for exams.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe or abhor something is to feel intense dislike for it.

parts.note: 're' means about or concerning, as in business letters
someone who is here is present, as when answering a register

explanation.surface: A museum label notes that an exhibit concerns this very place.
explanation.definitionFit: To portray or show something, as a painting does a scene, is a verb sense shared with exhibit.

indicators.note: 'in' tells us the letters for one's are placed inside the word for a job

parts.note: a post is a job or position
one's gives I

explanation.surface: Someone takes for granted that a person is already employed.
explanation.definitionFit: To put forward a premise as a basis for argument is to suppose or take it as given.

clue.text: Keeping pace, a creature crosses river

indicators.note: the creature word is laid across the river letter, so that letter sits inside it

parts.note: a beast is any animal or creature
R is the standard abbreviation for river on maps

explanation.surface: An animal swimming a river keeps up with its companions.
explanation.definitionFit: Being side by side and level with others is the literal sense of keeping up with them.

clue.text: Ringo is moving about his background

indicators.note: the letters of the drummer's name together with 'is' are shifted around into a new order

explanation.surface: Ringo Starr travels a lot, and that is somehow part of his story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is moving about' signals the anagram; RINGO plus IS gives the seven letters, and 'his background' describes Ringo's own roots.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's background is where they come from: their family, place and upbringing.

clue.text: Sack Sid, taken back to custody

indicators.note: the name Sid is turned around so its letters read in reverse order

parts.note: something in your charge is in your custody or care

explanation.surface: A man named Sid is dismissed and then returned to police custody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sack' looks like a noun for a bag but is the verb to dismiss; 'taken back' is the reversal signal on the name.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismiss someone from a job, informally to fire them, is a common sense of this verb.

clue.text: Impasse no longer fresh team needs replacing

parts.note: stale food is no longer fresh

indicators.note: the word team needs its letters replaced in a new order

explanation.surface: A tired sports side at a deadlock needs substitutes.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadlock where neither side can progress, borrowed from chess, is a standstill.

parts.note: a hunter of deer hopes to catch view of a female deer, and the same term means wisdom gained after the event

explanation.surface: Looking back, a hunter reflects on what he had hoped for.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'deerstalker' looks like the hat; here it is the hunter, whose aim is to spot a hind, a female deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Understanding of events only after they have happened is the wisdom of looking back.

parts.note: reads like a remark about a second career, but 'calling' means what you are called: a name that is not your main one

explanation.surface: Someone muses about a side job that isn't their main vocation.
explanation.definitionFit: An assumed name used instead of one's real one is a secondary name, not the main one.

parts.note: a gain is a profit or advantage

explanation.surface: A trader celebrates making money yet again.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something a second time, or another time, is doing it anew.

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill
costs are expenses

explanation.surface: Someone is faced with an invoice and charges.
explanation.definitionFit: To approach and address someone boldly or aggressively is to accost them.

clue.text: Pass the French fever to partner

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass
le is French for 'the'
ague is an old word for a malarial fever with shivering

explanation.surface: A warning not to spread a French illness to one's spouse.
explanation.definitionFit: A coworker or associate in a profession is someone you are partnered with at work.

parts.note: a blunder described as ringing out loudly, since the slang word for one comes from the noise of a metallic clang

explanation.surface: A blunder that was loud and very public.
explanation.walkthrough: British slang for a blunder, as in 'drop a clanger', is a loud ringing noise made by metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A conspicuous, embarrassing blunder is British slang dropped like a noisy object.

clue.text: Bird makes circuit over side of house

indicators.note: in a down answer, one piece placed over another comes first

parts.note: a lap is one circuit of a track
a wing is a side section of a large house

explanation.surface: A bird flies round once above one side of a mansion.
explanation.definitionFit: The peewit, a crested plover of fields, is a common wading bird.

parts.note: E for east is a compass point

indicators.note: a ruined garden is wrecked, so the letters of garden are mixed up

explanation.surface: Someone furiously points at a wrecked garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Being furious or incensed is being extremely angry.

clue.text: Potters about in a part of London?

definitions.text: Potters about in a part of London?

parts.words: Potters about in a part of London?
parts.note: 'potters' suggests people idling, but means makers of ceramics: an 18th-century porcelain works in a West London district was famous

explanation.surface: Someone pictures idlers strolling through a London neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potters about' suggests people dawdling; the potters are ceramic makers. The district is a smart area of West London whose 18th-century factory made famous porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: This riverside West London district gave its name to a celebrated soft-paste porcelain made there in the 1700s.

clue.text: Cat beginning to paw part of plant

indicators.note: the beginning of the word paw means only its opening letter is taken

parts.note: the anther is the pollen-bearing part of a flower's stamen

explanation.surface: A cat's first paw lands on part of a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A leopard, especially a black one, is a big wild feline.

parts.note: looks like a sibling's girlfriend, but means the daughter of one's brother

explanation.definitionFit: The daughter of one's sibling is a female relative one generation down.

parts.note: the slang order to go away, taken literally as jumping off on a single foot

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to depart while bouncing on a single foot.
explanation.walkthrough: British slang for 'go away!' is read literally here as departing by hopping.
explanation.definitionFit: A rude British instruction to clear off means go away.

indicators.note: only some of the letters in the words thieves' language are used, a run lying inside them

explanation.surface: A remark that thieves have a jargon of their own.
explanation.walkthrough: The word sits across the join of thieveS LANGuage, and the whole clue defines it, since the word first meant the cant of criminals.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal vocabulary originally meant the secret cant of criminals before broadening to any casual speech.

clue.text: Eat greedily put on over a pound as subject of experiment

indicators.note: in this across answer, one piece is put on, so it is placed after, the other

parts.note: a guinea was an old British coin worth 21 shillings, a little over a pound
to pig is to eat greedily, as in 'pig out'

explanation.surface: Someone stuffs themselves after putting on a pound, for science.
explanation.walkthrough: The GUINEA was an old British coin worth one pound and one shilling, hence 'over a pound'.
explanation.definitionFit: A person or thing tried out first, like the rodent used in laboratories, is a test subject.

indicators.note: 'out' suggests letters let loose and rearranged, so the words lets and her are mixed up

explanation.surface: Someone allows a woman to leave the port.
explanation.definitionFit: To give refuge or protect someone is to harbour them, a verb meaning to provide cover.

explanation.surface: Someone welcomed a visitor and burst into tears.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scotland and northern England 'greet' means to cry, a dialect sense many solvers will not know.
explanation.definitionFit: Saluted means welcomed with words or a gesture; 'greet' is also Scots for weep, so wept is its Scottish past tense.
